pull_requests.title: PERF Speed-up _weighted_percentiles when n_percentiles > 1
pull_requests.body:
`_weighted_percentile` loops over percentiles while every following operations can be vectorized. I just had to special case here and there the n_percentile = 1 case to avoid an unnecessary broadcast `(n_features, 1)` which would decrease the perfs for 1 percentile which is a very common use case of this function.
Here's the benchmark script that I used: ```py import csv import time import numpy as np from sklearn.utils.stats import _weighted_percentile N_SAMPLES = 10000 REPEATS = 100 def _make_data(n_features): rng = np.random.RandomState(0) shape = (N_SAMPLES, n_features) array = rng.normal(size=shape) weight = rng.uniform(0.1, 2.0, size=shape) return array, weight def _benchmark_case(array, weight, percentiles): for _ in range(5): _weighted_percentile(array, weight, percentiles, average=True) times = np.empty(REPEATS) for i in range(REPEATS): start = time.perf_counter() _weighted_percentile(array, weight, percentiles, average=True) times[i] = time.perf_counter() - start times = np.sort(times)[10:-10] # Drop the 10 fastest and 10 slowest. return np.median(times) def _write_grid_results(rows): path = f"bench_weighted_percentile_{N_SAMPLES}.csv" with open(path, "w", newline="") as f: writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0])) writer.writeheader() writer.writerows(rows) def benchmark_grid(): grid_n_features = (1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000) grid_n_percentiles = (1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000) rows = [] for n_features in grid_n_features: array, weight = _make_data(n_features) for n_percentiles in grid_n_percentiles: percentiles = ( np.linspace(0, 100, n_percentiles) if n_percentiles > 1 else 0.5 ) rows.append( { "n_features": n_features, "n_percentiles": n_percentiles, "time": _benchmark_case(array, weight, percentiles), } ) print(f"done {n_features=} | {n_percentiles=}") _write_grid_results(rows) ```
and the results for n_samples = 100 / 1000 / 10000 and various values for n_features and n_percentiles note that n_percentile = 1000 is the default for QuantileTransformer.

pull_requests.title: DOC clarify which imputers support categorical data
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #21722

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

The `impute` user guide did not say which estimators accept non-numeric data, which is the
single most common question about this module.

It now states that only `SimpleImputer` imputes non-numeric values, and only with the
`most_frequent` or `constant` strategy, while `IterativeImputer` and `KNNImputer` require
numeric input. A short example shows how to keep the missingness information with
`add_indicator`.

The statements were verified by running `SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")`,
`SimpleImputer(strategy="constant")`, `IterativeImputer()` and `KNNImputer()` on a mixed
`object`-dtype DataFrame, and `MissingIndicator(features="all")` on the same frame.

- Documentation (including examples)
- Research and understanding

pull_requests.title: DOC mention dual formulation in Ridge/RidgeClassifier solver docs
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #34807.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

The `solver` docstrings for `Ridge` (and `RidgeClassifier`, which shares the same solvers) did not mention that the 'cholesky' and 'sparse_cg' solvers switch between the primal and dual problem formulation depending on the shape of X. When `n_features > n_samples`, both solve the dual formulation based on the `n_samples x n_samples` kernel matrix `X @ X.T` instead of the primal formulation based on `X.T @ X`.

This documents existing behavior (verified in `ridge_regression` and `_solve_sparse_cg` in `sklearn/linear_model/_ridge.py`), following the precedent already set in the `RidgeCV` docstring for the 'eigen' solver.

Docs-only change; no runtime behavior modified.

#### Introduce yourself

I'm a software engineer at Meta (Instagram) and a long-time scikit-learn user. This is my first contribution to scikit-learn.

#### Any other comments?

Verified the updated docstrings parse cleanly with numpydoc and that all lines respect the 88-char limit.

pull_requests.title: FIX Improve error messages in StratifiedGroupKFold when y or groups is None (#30742)
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #30742

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`StratifiedGroupKFold.split` previously inherited `split` from `_BaseKFold`, where docstrings showed `y` and `groups` as optional with `default=None`. However, both parameters are mandatory:
- Omitting `y` led to an unhelpful `ValueError: Supported target types are: ('binary', 'multiclass'). Got 'unknown' instead.`
- Omitting `groups` led to `TypeError: iteration over a 0-d array` or a cryptic `ValueError` regarding split counts.

Following maintainer guidance on #30742 (matching `GroupKFold`):
1. In `StratifiedGroupKFold._iter_test_indices`:

pull_requests.title: BUG handle zero-count features in incremental variance
pull_requests.body:
## Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #35070

## What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`StandardScaler.partial_fit` can incorrectly replace an existing finite variance with `NaN` when a new dense batch contains no valid observations for a feature.

For example, if a feature has already accumulated statistics and a subsequent batch contains only `NaN` values for that feature, the incremental variance calculation can perform divisions by zero and propagate `NaN` into the stored variance and scale.

This PR fixes the dense `_incremental_mean_and_var` update by explicitly handling zero-count features.

### Changes

- Preserve the existing mean, variance, and count when a new batch has zero valid observations for a feature.
- Allow a feature with no previous observations to correctly establish its statistics when valid observations arrive in a later batch.
- Handle zero-weight batches without contributing to the incremental variance.
- Avoid unnecessary pooling and squared-value calculations for features with zero new observations.
- Explicitly represent mean and variance as `NaN` when the total observation count is zero.
- Add regression tests for weighted and unweighted inputs, zero-weight batches, first valid observations arriving later, large-mean overflow cases, and Array API zero-count combinations.

## Tests

Targeted tests and numerical checks were run for:

- Existing positive-count incremental variance paths.
- All four `(old_count, new_count)` combinations.
- Weighted and unweighted inputs.
- Zero-weight batches.
- Large-mean zero-new-observation cases.
- First valid observations arriving after an initially empty feature.
- Array API float32 and float64 cases.
- `git diff --check`.

A native pytest run of the checkout could not be completed in the current environment because the compiled scikit-learn build extension is unavailable. The targeted source-level tests passed.

## Additional notes

The fix is scoped to `_incremental_mean_and_var`. A separate overflow can occur later in `StandardScaler`'s `_is_constant_feature` calculation for extremely large means; that behavior is outside the scope of this issue.

pull_requests.title: Add uncertainty-coefficient normalizers to NMI
pull_requests.body:
## Summary

`normalized_mutual_info_score` could divide mutual information by a symmetric mean of the two entropies, but not by one entropy alone. Issue #12484 asks for the uncertainty coefficient: the fraction of `H(labels_true)` recovered by `labels_pred`.

- `average_method="labels_true"` returns `I(U; V) / H(U)`.
- `average_method="labels_pred"` returns `I(U; V) / H(V)`.

The four existing normalizers stay symmetric. These two are not. On the example from the issue, `[0, 1, 0, 1]` against `[0, 1, 0, 2]`, `labels_true` is 1 because the predicted labeling determines the reference, and `labels_pred` is `2/3`.

Adjusted mutual information is unchanged. Its chance correction is defined for a symmetric normalizer.

## Test plan

- [x] `test_nmi_uncertainty_coefficient` checks the issue example, `I / H(labels_pred)`, and the swapped call.
- [x] Loaded the edited module into scikit-learn 1.9.1 and got `labels_true = 1` and `labels_pred = 0.666...`.
- [ ] I did not run the full scikit-learn suite.

pull_requests.title: FIX Dont assume available CPU core count never changes
pull_requests.body:
Currently `_openmp_effective_n_threads()` assumes the number of available cores never changes.

This is not a correct assumption even now; the new test in this PR fails without the corresponding code changes. Changing CPU affinity at runtime is to be fair not very likely, even if it possible.

However, once joblib has a new release, this assumption will be a much bigger problem, since thread workers in `joblib.Parallel` will have different result in `cpu_count()` than e.g. the main thread. That is, `cpu_count()` will start being thread-local and tied to how many workers there are, with cores divided up between workers. See https://github.com/joblib/joblib/pull/1825 for details.

This PR therefore removes the caching.

#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #30223.


#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

The PR adds a new function to calculate accumulated local effects based on Apley and Zhu 2019: 

- paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.08468
- R implementation: https://github.com/cran/ALEPlot/blob/master/R/ALEPlot.R

Also discussed in https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/ale.html

#### Introduce yourself
<!-- Especially if you are new to the scikit-learn community, please introduce yourself.
How do you use scikit-learn, what prompted you to make this contribution?
Getting to know you helps us build trust in your judgement and welcome you into the
community.
-->

I am Sole, data scientist and Python dev. I met some of developers recently at Euroscipy 2026. 

I teach a course on interpretable machine learning, and while updating the course, I noticed that libraries that support ALE are either not being updated, or not fast enough, so given that sklearn already supports PDP and ICE, it felt natural that it should also support ALE, which is an alternative calculation of how feature value changes affect the model prediction.

#### AI usage disclosure
<!--
Edit the list below to show when/how you used AI tools to create this PR.
Keep the ones that apply, delete the rest.
Make sure that you adhere to our Automated Contributions Policy:
https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#automated-contributions-policy
-->

I use Claude Opus 5.5 to start off and then I review every line.

#### Any other comments?

While creating the first draft I came across some issues that need resolving.

**NAN values**. The problem arises when models support nan values, like tree based models, because it is not clear which values should be used to replace those nan. 

Briefly, ale sorts values into intervals. Then replaces each sample value with the interval edges (2 replacements), it obtains the predictions, and the local effect is the prediction at the maximum value minus the prediction at the minimum value. Pretty much like PDP, but PDP replaces all samples with the same value. Here, we'd replace each sample with 2 values only, min edge and max edge.

The problem with nan is, that it's not clear which value should be used for replacement, because it can't fall into any bin. So my first suggestion would be to exclude nan from the calculation, even if they can be used by the model.

The second problem (not a big one) is how to handle categorical variables. The original paper and molnar's book suggests a way in which to assign order to the categories based on feature proximity. I'd say that's out of scope and we outsource that problem to the user.

**discrete/categorical variables**: The next question is, how do we calculate the effects for **discrete/categorical variables**. The paper does not describe it clearly, but the R implementation does. This is what basically took most of my time to understand, because, no matter how long I think about it, it doesn't make a lot of sense in my head. 
We have 2 options here:

- Option 1 would be to just do what the author did. 
- Option 2, not to support discrete variables.

This is still WIP.

pull_requests.title: Store all fitted attributes as Numpy arrays
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34604

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This adds a class that proxies access to fitted attributes and moves them to the required namespace/device on access.

It is a way to implement what https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34604 proposes. Namely store all fitted attributes as numpy arrays and then convert them to the namespace/device of `X` on the fly when they are used in `predict`, `score`, `transform`, etc.

The fundamental idea of this PR is to provide a class `_FittedAttrsLike` that can be used in `predict` to give access to the attributes and take care of the conversions (and caching of those).

```python
def predict(self, X):
  # Use `fitted` like `self` to access fitted attributes
  fitted = _fitted_attrs_like(self, X)
  # This used to be:  return X @ self.coef_.T + self.intercept_
  return X @ fitted.coef_.T + fitted.intercept_
```

The second part of this PR is `_fitted_attrs_as_numpy(estimator)` which modifies an estimator in place and moves all of its fitted attributes to numpy. It is called at the end of the `_fit_context` decorator. This means we don't have to modify `fit`/add boiler plate code to `fit` (or forget to do that). `_fitted_attrs_as_numpy` is almost equal to `move_estimator_to`, the difference is that it modifies the estimator in place instead of `clone`ing.

The third part of this PR is adding a shortcut to `move_to` for the case were both source and target are numpy. Some of the functions we call and determinations we have to make as part of the general case in `move_to` are "expensive". Because the `_fitted_attrs_as_numpy()` call lives in `_fit_context` it gets applied to estimators with no array API support. So it felt worth adding this short cut to keep the overhead small. There is also https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34840 which explores making micro optimisations for `move_to()`.

This PR converts a few classes to use this pattern. Mostly to avoid having a gigantic diff while we decide on the API. It also adjusts the common tests/checks. Until all estimators have been converted to this pattern we need a list to keep track which estimators use this pattern and which don't.

This is an alternative to https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34667 which was a first attempt of implementing this. I think I prefer the API and ergonomics of this PR

pull_requests.title: DOC clarify the LARS coefficient path description in the user guide
pull_requests.body:
Fixes #32083

## Why

The "Mathematical formulation" dropdown of the LARS Lasso user guide section describes "the LARS solution" as "a curve denoting the solution for each value of the l1 norm". Issue #32083 points out that this is unclear: "the LARS solution" is not a defined term here, a path is not a curve "computed at every point", and nothing says which attribute stores the result.

The suggested replacement in the issue fixes the vagueness but reintroduces a shape claim `(n_features, max_features + 1)`. That formula does not match the API documentation of `coef_path_` (`array-like of shape (n_features, n_alphas + 1)`), and it breaks down in the truncated case: with `Lars(n_nonzero_coefs=1)` on a 5-sample problem, `coef_path_` has 2 columns while `alphas_` has size 2 (and `max_features` is 1, so the issue's formula would predict 2 as well - the two documented formulas disagree with each other and with the implementation in different regimes).

## What

Rewrite the paragraph to:

- say explicitly that LARS yields a whole coefficient path with one coefficient vector per breakpoint, instead of the undefined term "the LARS solution";
- point to the `coef_path_` attribute of `Lars` / `LassoLars` via `:class:` references, consistent with the rest of the file;
- not restate the shape in the user guide, deferring to the API docs where it is maintained (and where the multi-target list case is already documented).

Verified locally (sklearn 1.8.0): `coef_path_[:, 0]` is all zero for both `Lars` and `LassoLars`; `coef_` equals the last path column; multi-target fits return a list of arrays.

Only the user guide paragraph is changed; the docstrings are untouched.

pull_requests.title: PERF Speed up kdtree when distance metric's p is 1 or 2
pull_requests.body:
While poking around at a profile output for the example referenced in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/25812 I noticed that `pow()` was using a lot of time.

Since the exponent is usually `dist_metric.p`, which is in most is cases 1 or 2, this allows for a fast path to skip the overhead of calling `pow`. INF case is already bypassed by these codepaths.

Thus, the only case which is getting more overhead is when it's `1 / dist_metric.p` and `p` is 2, and `MinkowskiDistance` which can accept arbitrary positive floats for `p`.


#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
No need to call `pow()` when exponent is 1 or 2.

#### Benchmarks
Derived from skops repo's history:

```python
from time import perf_counter

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
```

`from sklearn.model_selection import *` has raised `ImportError` since 1.8.0: PR #31847 listed `HalvingGridSearchCV` and `HalvingRandomSearchCV` in `__all__`, while the module's `__getattr__` deliberately raises `ImportError` for both until `enable_halving_search_cv` is imported. - the experimental estimators remain reachable via `enable_halving_search_cv` as documented.

- Added `sklearn/model_selection/tests/test_star_import.py`: star-import in a fresh subprocess succeeds; the two names are absent from `__all__`; explicit access still raises the guidance error.

pull_requests.title: Fix normalized BayesianRidge scores_ (#13852)
pull_requests.body:
Fixes #13852.

### Why

`BayesianRidge.scores_` includes the Gaussian likelihood constant but omits the normalization constants of its two Gamma priors. This makes scores incomplete when comparing different prior hyperparameters. The final score also needs to use the final fitted coefficients.

### Derivation

For unweighted data with `fit_intercept=False`, let `n` be the number of samples and `p` the number of features. With `A = lambda I + alpha X.T X` and `mu = alpha A^{-1} X.T y`, integrating out the coefficients gives

```
log p(y | X, alpha, lambda)
= 1/2 [p log(lambda) + n log(alpha) - log|A|
       - alpha ||y - X mu||^2 - lambda ||mu||^2 - n log(2 pi)].
```

The documented Gamma priors have shapes `alpha_1` and `lambda_1` and rates `alpha_2` and `lambda_2`. For a precision `t` with shape `a` and rate `b`, let `u = log(t)`. The density in log-precision coordinates includes the change-of-variable Jacobian:

```
log p(u) = a log(t) - b t + a log(b) - log Gamma(a).
```

The existing score contains `a log(t) - b t`, so this change adds `a log(b) - log Gamma(a)` when both `a` and `b` are positive. If either is zero, the prior is improper and its undefined normalization constant is omitted. With `fit_intercept=False`, `sample_weight=None`, and proper priors, `scores_` is a normalized joint log density of `y`, `log(alpha)`, and `log(lambda)` given `X`.

### Changes

- Add the Gamma normalization constants for proper priors without changing the fitting updates or predictions.
- Evaluate the final score with the final fitted coefficients.
- Rename the private score method to `_log_joint_score` and clarify the score documentation.
- Compare initial and final scores with independent SciPy Gaussian and Gamma log densities for both `n > p` and `p > n`. Test zero-shape and zero-rate priors separately.

### Verification

All 32 tests in `sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_bayes.py` passed with the modified source module loaded against the installed scikit-learn 1.8 runtime. This source checkout lacks compiled extensions, so its native test invocation was unavailable. Ruff formatting, selected lint checks, and `git diff --check` passed.

#### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm Luis. I really like scikit-learn and wanted to start contributing to it. I looked for smaller issues I could understand and solve carefully, with the hope of taking on more complex work as I get to know the codebase. This BayesianRidge issue caught my attention because it let me work through the mathematics and make a focused improvement.

pull_requests.title: FIX: raise clean ValueError in _resize_state when shrinking n_estimators
pull_requests.body:
### PR summary

`BaseGradientBoosting._resize_state` guards against shrinking
`n_estimators`, but formatted the error message with
`self.estimators_[0]` — the first fitted estimator object — instead of
`self.estimators_.shape[0]` (the count). Since `%d` cannot format a
non-numeric object, the intended `ValueError` crashed with a confusing
`TypeError: %d format: a real number is required, not numpy.ndarray`.

The branch is currently unreachable through the public `fit()` API (the
outer warm-start check raises first), which is why the existing
`test_warm_start_smaller_n_estimators` never caught it. The fix corrects
the variable and adds a parametrized regression test that calls
`_resize_state` directly for both `GradientBoostingClassifier` and
`GradientBoostingRegressor`.

Closes #34496.

### Testing

- New `test_resize_state_smaller_n_estimators`: fails on the old code
  with the reported `TypeError`, passes with the fix (clean `ValueError`
  with message `resize with smaller n_estimators 5 < 10`).

pull_requests.title: DOC Clarify n_jobs in BaggingClassifier and BaggingRegressor
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Refs #14228. The new wording is modeled on the RandomForest `n_jobs` docstring from #14628.


#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

This PR only changes the `n_jobs` description in `BaggingClassifier` and `BaggingRegressor`.

The current text says jobs run in parallel "for both fit and predict". That doesn't tell the reader what gets split across the jobs, and for the classifier it misses `predict_proba`, `predict_log_proba` and `decision_function`, which also run in parallel.

The new text names every parallel method and says the work is parallelized by splitting the base estimators across jobs. RandomForest says "over the trees", but Bagging hands each job a group of estimators, so I went with "splitting the base estimators across jobs". `_partition_estimators` makes `min(n_jobs, n_estimators)` groups, which means an `n_jobs` larger than `n_estimators` gives no extra speed-up. The sentences about `None`, `-1` and the Glossary are unchanged.

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_base.py#L171-L181

Where each method runs in parallel:

- `fit`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L541
- `predict_proba` (classifier `predict` calls it): https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1025
- `predict_log_proba`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1099
- `decision_function`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1176
- regressor `predict`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1433

I also timed each method at `n_jobs` 1, 2, 4 and 6 on my own machine (Windows 11, 6 physical cores, scikit-learn 1.10.dev0 built from `4358542`). Every run used `n_estimators=100` with the default trees, and each number is the median of 5 runs after a warm-up. Trees don't have a `decision_function`, so that row uses `SVC` as the base estimator. The last row is a control. With a KNN base estimator and `oob_score=True`, most of `fit` is OOB scoring, and its time doesn't drop as `n_jobs` goes up. Times are in seconds.

| Method | n_jobs=1 | n_jobs=2 | n_jobs=4 | n_jobs=6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `BaggingClassifier.fit` | 3.65 | 2.04 | 1.08 | 0.72 |
| `BaggingClassifier.predict` | 1.48 | 0.90 | 0.61 | 0.57 |
| `BaggingClassifier.predict_proba` | 1.32 | 0.83 | 0.60 | 0.57 |
| `BaggingClassifier.predict_log_proba` | 1.79 | 1.23 | 0.75 | 0.64 |
| `BaggingClassifier(SVC()).decision_function` | 4.28 | 2.48 | 1.60 | 1.19 |
| `BaggingRegressor.fit` | 3.73 | 2.08 | 1.23 | 0.86 |
| `BaggingRegressor.predict` | 1.89 | 1.26 | 0.87 | 0.78 |
| Control: `BaggingClassifier(KNeighborsClassifier(), oob_score=True).fit` | 3.19 | 3.49 | 3.43 | 3.40 |

<details>
<summary>Timing script</summary>

```python
r"""Local evidence for the n_jobs docstrings of BaggingClassifier and BaggingRegressor.

Times each public method at several n_jobs values through the public API only,
plus two controls that n_jobs should not speed up. Kept outside the scikit-learn
clone.

Usage (--calibrate times each step once at n_jobs=1, to pick data sizes):

    python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --calibrate
    python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --clf-samples 2500 --reg-samples 3000 \
        --predict-samples 60000 --svc-test 1000 --knn-samples 7500
"""

import argparse
import contextlib
import io
import os
import statistics
import time
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import joblib

import sklearn
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification, make_regression
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, BaggingRegressor
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier, KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.svm import SVC

N_JOBS = [1, 2, 4, 6]  # 6 = physical core count of the test machine
N_REPEATS = 5
N_ESTIMATORS = 100
N_FEATURES = 20
RANDOM_STATE = 0
RESULTS_FILE = Path(__file__).with_name("bagging_n_jobs_results.md")

# Thresholds for the pass/FAIL checks
CLEARLY_FASTER = 0.8  # at 2 jobs, a method must take under 80% of its 1-job time
NOISE = 1.1  # a higher n_jobs may be at most 10% slower than the previous one
OOB_FLAT = 0.7  # KNN fit (mostly OOB scoring) must stay above 70% of its 1-job time
CAP_FLAT = 0.9  # with 2 estimators, 4 and 6 jobs must stay above 90% of 2 jobs


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--calibrate", action="store_true",
                        help="time each step once at n_jobs=1 to size the data")
    parser.add_argument("--clf-samples", type=int, default=8_000,
                        help="training samples for BaggingClassifier")
    parser.add_argument("--reg-samples", type=int, default=8_000,
                        help="training samples for BaggingRegressor")
    parser.add_argument("--predict-samples", type=int, default=50_000,
                        help="samples passed to the prediction methods")
    parser.add_argument("--svc-train", type=int, default=2_000,
                        help="training samples for the SVC decision_function run")
    parser.add_argument("--svc-test", type=int, default=5_000,
                        help="samples passed to decision_function")
    parser.add_argument("--knn-samples", type=int, default=6_000,
                        help="training samples for the KNN OOB control")
    return parser.parse_args()


def make_data(args):
    """Synthetic data, split into a training part and a prediction part."""
    Xc, yc = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.clf_samples + args.predict_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xr, yr = make_regression(
        n_samples=args.reg_samples + args.predict_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, noise=10.0, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xs, ys = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.svc_train + args.svc_test, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xkc, ykc = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.knn_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES, n_informative=10,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xkr, ykr = make_regression(
        n_samples=args.knn_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES, n_informative=10,
        noise=10.0, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    n, m, s = args.clf_samples, args.reg_samples, args.svc_train
    return {
        "clf": (Xc[:n], yc[:n], Xc[n:]),
        "reg": (Xr[:m], yr[:m], Xr[m:]),
        "svc": (Xs[:s], ys[:s], Xs[s:]),
        "knn_clf": (Xkc, ykc),
        "knn_reg": (Xkr, ykr),
    }


def run_once(func):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    func()
    return time.perf_counter() - start


def median_time(func):
    """Median wall-clock time of func() over N_REPEATS runs, after one warm-up."""
    func()  # warm-up: starts the worker processes; not recorded
    return statistics.median(run_once(func) for _ in range(N_REPEATS))


def time_fit(label, estimator_class, X, y, **params):
    """Time fit on a fresh estimator for each n_jobs value."""
    print(f"timing {label} ...", flush=True)
    times = {}
    for n in N_JOBS:
        estimator = estimator_class(n_jobs=n, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, **params)
        times[n] = median_time(lambda: estimator.fit(X, y))
    return times


def time_method(label, fitted, method, X):
    """Time one prediction method of a fitted estimator for each n_jobs value."""
    print(f"timing {label} ...", flush=True)
    times = {}
    for n in N_JOBS:
        fitted.set_params(n_jobs=n)
        times[n] = median_time(lambda: getattr(fitted, method)(X))
    return times


def fit_for_prediction(estimator):
    """Fit once with all jobs; prediction timings then change n_jobs only."""
    return estimator.set_params(n_jobs=max(N_JOBS))


# --- go/no-go checks --------------------------------------------------------


def is_parallel(times):
    """Clearly faster at 2 jobs than at 1, and never slower as n_jobs rises."""
    t = [times[n] for n in N_JOBS]
    return t[1] < CLEARLY_FASTER * t[0] and all(
        later <= NOISE * earlier for earlier, later in zip(t, t[1:])
    )


def stays_flat(times):
    """A fit that is mostly OOB scoring does not get faster as n_jobs rises."""
    base = times[N_JOBS[0]]
    return base > 0 and all(times[n] >= OOB_FLAT * base for n in N_JOBS)


def capped_at_two(times):
    """With 2 estimators, more than 2 jobs gives no further speed-up."""
    return all(times[n] >= CAP_FLAT * times[2] for n in N_JOBS if n > 2)


# --- modes ------------------------------------------------------------------


def calibrate(data):
    """Single runs at n_jobs=1, to pick data sizes before the full run."""
    X, y, X_pred = data["clf"]
    clf = BaggingClassifier(n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, n_jobs=1,
                            random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    print(f"BaggingClassifier.fit            {run_once(lambda: clf.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s"
          "  (target 3-5 s)")
    print(f"BaggingClassifier.predict_proba  "
          f"{run_once(lambda: clf.predict_proba(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    X, y, X_pred = data["reg"]
    reg = BaggingRegressor(n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, n_jobs=1,
                           random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    print(f"BaggingRegressor.fit             {run_once(lambda: reg.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s"
          "  (target 3-5 s)")
    print(f"BaggingRegressor.predict         "
          f"{run_once(lambda: reg.predict(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    X, y, X_pred = data["svc"]
    svc = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        SVC(), n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X, y)
    svc.set_params(n_jobs=1)
    print(f"BaggingClassifier(SVC()).decision_function "
          f"{run_once(lambda: svc.decision_function(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    for name, estimator_class, knn, (X, y) in [
        ("BaggingClassifier", BaggingClassifier, KNeighborsClassifier(), data["knn_clf"]),
        ("BaggingRegressor", BaggingRegressor, KNeighborsRegressor(), data["knn_reg"]),
    ]:
        est = estimator_class(knn, n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, oob_score=True,
                              n_jobs=1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
        print(f"{name}(KNN).fit, oob_score=True "
              f"{run_once(lambda: est.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s  (target 3-5 s)")


def full_run(data):
    """Time every documented method and both controls; return table rows."""
    rows = []  # (label, times, check or None)

    X, y, X_pred = data["clf"]
    rows.append(("BaggingClassifier.fit",
                 time_fit("BaggingClassifier.fit", BaggingClassifier, X, y,
                          n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS),
                 is_parallel))
    clf = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X, y)
    for method in ["predict", "predict_proba", "predict_log_proba"]:
        label = f"BaggingClassifier.{method}"
        rows.append((label, time_method(label, clf, method, X_pred), is_parallel))

    X_svc, y_svc, X_svc_pred = data["svc"]
    svc = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        SVC(), n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X_svc, y_svc)
    label = "BaggingClassifier(SVC()).decision_function"
    rows.append((label, time_method(label, svc, "decision_function", X_svc_pred),
                 is_parallel))

    Xr, yr, Xr_pred = data["reg"]
    rows.append(("BaggingRegressor.fit",
                 time_fit("BaggingRegressor.fit", BaggingRegressor, Xr, yr,
                          n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS),
                 is_parallel))
    reg = fit_for_prediction(BaggingRegressor(
        n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(Xr, yr)
    label = "BaggingRegressor.predict"
    rows.append((label, time_method(label, reg, "predict", Xr_pred), is_parallel))

    # Control 1: OOB scoring runs sequentially at the end of fit. KNN fits almost
    # instantly but is slow to predict, so this fit is mostly OOB scoring.
    for name, estimator_class, knn, (Xk, yk) in [
        ("BaggingClassifier", BaggingClassifier, KNeighborsClassifier(), data["knn_clf"]),
        ("BaggingRegressor", BaggingRegressor, KNeighborsRegressor(), data["knn_reg"]),
    ]:
        label = f"Control: {name}(KNN).fit, oob_score=True"
        rows.append((label,
                     time_fit(label, estimator_class, Xk, yk, estimator=knn,
                              n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, oob_score=True),
                     stays_flat))

    # Control 2: estimators are split into at most n_estimators groups
    label = "Control: BaggingClassifier.fit, n_estimators=2"
    rows.append((label, time_fit(label, BaggingClassifier, X, y, n_estimators=2),
                 capped_at_two))
    return rows


# --- report -----------------------------------------------------------------


def format_table(rows):
    first, last = N_JOBS[0], N_JOBS[-1]
    lines = [
        "| Timing (s) | " + " | ".join(f"n_jobs={n}" for n in N_JOBS)
        + f" | Speed-up {first} to {last} | Check |",
        "|---" * (len(N_JOBS) + 3) + "|",
    ]
    for label, times, check in rows:
        cells = " | ".join(f"{times[n]:.3f}" for n in N_JOBS)
        speedup = f"{times[first] / times[last]:.2f}x" if times[last] > 0 else "n/a"
        result = "" if check is None else ("pass" if check(times) else "FAIL")
        lines.append(f"| {label} | {cells} | {speedup} | {result} |")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def environment_report():
    buffer = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer):
        sklearn.show_versions()
    return (f"Physical cores (joblib): {joblib.cpu_count(only_physical_cores=True)}\n"
            f"Logical cores (os): {os.cpu_count()}\n{buffer.getvalue()}")


def main():
    args = parse_args()
    data = make_data(args)
    if args.calibrate:
        calibrate(data)
        return

    rows = full_run(data)
    all_pass = all(check(times) for _, times, check in rows if check is not None)
    report = "\n\n".join([
        f"# Bagging n_jobs timing, {datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}",
        f"Settings: {vars(args)}, n_estimators={N_ESTIMATORS}, "
        f"n_features={N_FEATURES}, median of {N_REPEATS} runs after 1 warm-up, "
        "default joblib backend.",
        format_table(rows),
        f"Automatic checks: {'all pass (go)' if all_pass else 'some FAIL (review)'}",
        f"## Environment\n\n```\n{environment_report()}```",
    ])
    RESULTS_FILE.write_text(report + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("\n" + format_table(rows))
    print(f"\nAutomatic checks: {'all pass' if all_pass else 'some FAIL'}")
    print(f"Saved to {RESULTS_FILE}")


if __name__ == "__main__":  # required on Windows: joblib starts new processes
    main()
```

Run with: `python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --clf-samples 2500 --reg-samples 3000 --predict-samples 60000 --svc-test 1000 --knn-samples 7500`

</details>

I wasn't sure whether the docstring should mention OOB scoring. With `oob_score=True`, the OOB step at the end of `fit` is a plain `for` loop over the estimators, so `n_jobs` doesn't speed it up. That's what the control row shows. I left it out to keep the docstring short and in line with RandomForest. Should I add a short note about it?

- OOB loop, classifier: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L896
- OOB loop, regressor: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1454


#### Introduce yourself

I'm Nitin Mishra, a B.Tech student in Computer Science and AI at Tensor School of Computer Science and AI. I use scikit-learn in my ML trading projects and I'm interested in contributing to open source. I picked #14228 because it's a small docs change with a clear scope, and I could check it against the code and measure it on my own machine. This isn't my first PR, but feedback on how I could do better is very welcome. So are pointers on where to learn more and how to get to know other contributors.

Fixes #34883

When `classes` contains string labels that parse as integers (e.g. `"1"`, `"2"`), `compute_class_weight` was coercing them to integers via `int(c)`, which then failed to match the string keys in `class_weight`.

pull_requests.title: FIX confusion_matrix_at_thresholds precision loss on plain numpy with float32 y_score
pull_requests.body:
Fixes #34975.

PR #34817 fixed a precision-loss bug in `confusion_matrix_at_thresholds`'s unweighted branch for restricted array-API devices that don't support `float64`, by computing the cumulative true-positive/false-positive counts exactly in `int64` before casting to a float output dtype. But the cast picked `output_dtype = y_score.dtype` whenever `y_score` is real-floating, instead of the device's max-precision float dtype (`_max_precision_float_dtype(xp, device)`, already computed as the fallback for non-floating `y_score`).

On plain numpy, `_max_precision_float_dtype` is always `float64` — but if the caller's `y_score` happens to be `float32` (e.g. model scores stored in `float32` to save memory, a very common case), the exact `int64` counts were still needlessly downcast to `float32`, which cannot represent integers exactly above `2**24` (~16.7M). This reintroduced exactly the bug class #34817 was fixing, just for ordinary numpy with a float32 *input* rather than a float32-only *device*. The weighted branch immediately below doesn't have this problem — it already always uses `max_float_dtype` regardless of `y_score`'s dtype.

This affects `confusion_matrix_at_thresholds`, `roc_curve`, `precision_recall_curve`, `det_curve`, and `roc_auc_score`.

## Fix

Use `_max_precision_float_dtype(xp, device)` unconditionally for `output_dtype` in the unweighted branch, matching the weighted branch. This is strictly more correct: on devices where max precision actually is `float32`, behavior is unchanged; on any device (including plain numpy) where `float64` is available, output is now always the exact count regardless of `y_score`'s dtype.

## Test plan

- [x] Added `test_confusion_matrix_at_thresholds_float32_y_score_plain_numpy_exact`, reproducing the exact scenario from the issue on plain numpy (20M samples, `float32` `y_score`) — confirmed it fails on the pre-fix code (temporarily reverted the fix to verify) before restoring it.
- [x] The existing array-API restricted-device test added by #34817 (`test_confusion_matrix_at_thresholds_float32_only_unweighted_large_n`) still passes unchanged, confirming this doesn't regress that fix.
- [x] `pytest sklearn/metrics/tests/test_ranking.py` → 249 passed.
- [x] `SCIPY_ARRAY_API=1 pytest sklearn/metrics/tests/test_ranking.py sklearn/metrics/tests/test_common.py -k "roc or auc or det_curve or precision_recall or confusion_matrix_at_thresholds"` → 253 passed.
- [x] `ruff check`/`ruff format --check` clean (project's pinned `ruff==0.12.2`).
- [x] Added a changelog entry under `doc/whats_new/upcoming_changes/sklearn.metrics/34975.fix.rst`.

cc @ogrisel as requested on the issue.

---

I used Claude (Anthropic) to help investigate this issue (an open-ended search for an unreported bug that led here), design and implement the fix, and verify it against existing/new tests including confirming non-vacuousness. I reviewed, tested, and understand the change before submitting it under my name, per the project's Automated Contributions Policy.

pull_requests.title: FIX Pipeline step names are lost for non-composite steps in HTML repr
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs Addresses one item of #32146 ("`Pipeline` doesn't display its named steps"). #### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes. `Pipeline._sk_visual_block_` builds a `"step_name: ClassName"` label for each of its steps (see `_get_name` in `sklearn/pipeline.py`), but the HTML diagram never showed it for a step whose estimator is not itself a meta-estimator: ```python from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression())]) ``` Before this fix, the diagram showed the boxes `StandardScaler` and `LogisticRegression`, with the step names `scaler`/`clf` nowhere to be seen (they only survived in the non-HTML fallback `
` text and in the
`data-param-prefix` attribute used by the copy-to-clipboard feature).

Root cause, in `_write_estimator_html`
(`sklearn/utils/_repr_html/estimator.py`): when the current node is a
`"single"` (leaf, non-composite) block, the function always used
`est_block.names`, i.e. the leaf's *own* `_get_visual_block` result. For a
plain estimator with no `_sk_visual_block_` of its own, that is always
just `estimator.__class__.__name__` (see the generic fallback at the
bottom of `_get_visual_block`). The `estimator_label` parameter carrying
the parent's `"step_name: ClassName"` label was passed into the function
but silently discarded in this branch. The parent's label *was* used
correctly for `"serial"`/`"parallel"` (i.e. nested meta-estimator) blocks,
just not for plain leaves, which is why the bug was easy to miss.

The fix restores the parent-provided label specifically for the case that
was losing it: a leaf estimator that has no `_sk_visual_block_` of its
own (i.e. is not a string, not `None`, and not a meta-estimator). Two
existing behaviors are preserved on purpose:
- `passthrough`/`None` steps keep showing the bare `"passthrough"` label
  (they are handled as a dedicated special case both here and in
  `_write_label_html`, and there's already an existing test pinning this).
- Estimators that define their own `_sk_visual_block_`, such as
  `FunctionTransformer`, keep their own label (e.g. the wrapped function's
  name) instead of being overridden by the step name, since they already
  carry their own intended display in `est_block.names`.

`TransformedTargetRegressor._sk_visual_block_` builds the exact same kind
of `"regressor: ClassName"` label for its wrapped regressor and hits the
same code path, so it is fixed the same way as a side effect.

#### Testing
- Added `test_estimator_html_repr_pipeline_step_names` in
  `sklearn/utils/_repr_html/tests/test_estimator.py`, covering: a plain
  step showing `"name: ClassName"`, a `passthrough` step keeping its bare
  label, `TransformedTargetRegressor`, and a `FunctionTransformer` step
  keeping its own function-name label.
- Updated `test_search_html_repr` in
  `sklearn/model_selection/tests/test_search.py`: its assertions checked
  for the bare class name (e.g. `"
DummyClassifier
"`) as a
  substring, which happened to still match inside the old,
  incorrectly-shortened label. With the fix the label is now the correct,
  longer `"clf: DummyClassifier"`, so the assertions are updated to check
  for that instead.
- `pytest sklearn/utils/_repr_html/ sklearn/tests/test_pipeline.py
  sklearn/compose/ sklearn/ensemble/
  sklearn/model_selection/tests/test_search.py
  sklearn/feature_selection/ sklearn/tests/test_calibration.py` passes
  (2056 passed, 477 skipped, 0 failed).
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are clean on the changed files.

#### Introduce yourself
Hi, I'm a first-year CS student who's been using scikit-learn for coursework
and wanted to make a real contribution back. I ran into #32146 while reading
through the HTML repr code and traced this particular checklist item (the
missing Pipeline step names) down to the root cause described above. This
is my first PR to scikit-learn.

#### AI usage disclosure
I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (e.g., when writing an implementation or fixing a bug)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Research and understanding

I reviewed the diff, understand the root cause and the fix, and ran the
test suite and linters listed above myself before opening this PR.

#### Any other comments?
Happy to adjust the approach (e.g. also namespacing `FunctionTransformer`
steps as `"name: FunctionTransformer(...)"` ) if maintainers prefer a
different scope than "only fix the leaves that were losing information
outright".

pull_requests.title: ﻿FIX RidgeClassifierCV scoring with cv=None for binary classification
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #34942


#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
Fixes `RidgeClassifierCV(scoring=..., cv=None)` returning `best_score_ = 1.0`
for all binary classification problems.

**Root cause.** In `_RidgeGCV._score` (`sklearn/linear_model/_ridge.py`),
class labels were reconstructed with `xp.argmax(y, axis=1)`.
`LabelBinarizer(pos_label=1, neg_label=-1)` produces a **single-column**
target for binary problems, so `argmax(axis=1)` was always 0. Both `y_true`
and `y_pred` therefore collapsed to `classes_[0]`, and any classifier scorer
(`accuracy_score`, `f1`, etc.) returned 1.0 or otherwise degenerate values.
Multiclass was unaffected because `argmax` on the one-hot matrix is correct.

**Fix.** Handle the binary case explicitly inside `_RidgeGCV._score`:
- map the sign of `y` to class indices 0/1: `y_true = (y > 0).astype(int)`
- reshape the single-column decision values into a two-column layout so the
  usual argmax-based class inference in `_IdentityClassifier.predict` works
- leave the multiclass path unchanged

**Tests.** Added three regression tests to
`sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_ridge.py`:
- `test_ridge_classifier_cv_binary_scoring_accuracy` — asserts `best_score_`
  is strictly between 0 and 1 on random binary data
- `test_ridge_classifier_cv_binary_scoring_matches_cv` — asserts GCV and
  explicit `cv=5` scores agree within 0.2
- `test_ridge_classifier_cv_multiclass_scoring_still_works` — guards against
  regressions in the multiclass path

Full `pytest sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_ridge.py` locally:
`1093 passed, 346 skipped, 54 xfailed`.


#### Introduce yourself
Hi, I'm Abdelrahman Adel, a developer based in Egypt. I use scikit-learn for
classical machine learning baselines in my projects and was working with
`RidgeClassifierCV` as a classifier head when I noticed that binary
problems always reported `best_score_ = 1.0`, which made the model-selection
step effectively a no-op for those cases. Tracing the behaviour led me to
`_RidgeGCV._score`, where the label reconstruction relies on
`xp.argmax(y, axis=1)` — which is meaningless for the single-column
binarized target used in binary classification.

This is my first contribution to scikit-learn. I'm happy to adjust the fix,
the tests, or the approach itself if maintainers prefer a different
structure. Thanks for taking the time to review.


#### AI usage disclosure
I used AI assistance for:
- Research and understanding (locating the root cause and cross-checking
  how `LabelBinarizer` interacts with `argmax`)
- Code generation (draft of the fix in `_RidgeGCV._score`)
- Test generation (drafts of the three regression tests)

I have reviewed the final diff, run the full `test_ridge.py` module
locally (`1093 passed, 346 skipped, 54 xfailed`), and verified the fix
reproduces the expected behaviour with the original issue's reproducer.
I understand and follow the Automated Contributions Policy.


#### Any other comments?
The issue was labeled "Needs triage" when I started; I commented on
#34942 before opening this PR. I'm happy to split or restructure the
change if a maintainer prefers a different approach (e.g. always
converting `y` to a two-column layout for classifiers, or adding an
explicit `is_binary` branch in `_RidgeClassifierMixin`). Thanks for
reviewing.

pull_requests.title: FIX SpectralEmbedding to work with sparse array backend with large indices
pull_requests.body:
This was triggered during an update to skops to support scipy=2, where testing for sparse arrays caused an error with `SpectralEmbedding`. This fixes the issue.

#### AI usage disclosure
<!--
Edit the list below to show when/how you used AI tools to create this PR.
Keep the ones that apply, delete the rest.
Make sure that you adhere to our Automated Contributions Policy:
https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#automated-contributions-policy
-->
I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (e.g., when writing an implementation or fixing a bug)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Documentation (including examples)
- Research and understanding

#### Any other comments?

Claude's summary:

<details>

SpectralEmbedding.fit (and SpectralClustering, which shares the same code path) builds its graph Laplacian from a k-NN sparse graph. Under sparse_interface="sparray", that graph ends up with int64 indices — not because scikit-learn does anything different, but because of a deliberate scipy design choice: sparse arrays (csr_array, unlike csr_matrix) never downcast index dtype based on content when built from raw (data, indices, indptr) arrays (scipy/scipy#16774). kneighbors_graph constructs its output that way, so the int64 propagates through 0.5 * (A + A.T) and csgraph_laplacian too.

The eigen_solver="arpack" branch in sklearn/manifold/_spectral_embedding.py then called check_array(laplacian, accept_sparse="csr", accept_large_sparse=False), rejecting those int64 indices — a restriction the "amg" and "lobpcg" branches in the same file don't impose. I confirmed scipy.sparse.linalg.eigsh, including the shift-invert mode used here (sigma=-1e-5), works fine with int64-indexed sparse arrays, so the restriction was just overly conservative, not load-bearing.

Fix

Dropped accept_large_sparse=False from that one check_array call in sklearn/manifold/_spectral_embedding.py:372 (defaults to True, matching the other two solver branches). Added a regression test comparing SpectralEmbedding output between sparse_interface="spmatrix" and "sparray", and a changelog fragment (doc/whats_new/upcoming_changes/sklearn.manifold/34959.fix.rst — PR number guessed as the next available; adjust once the real PR is opened).

Verified: the reproducer from the issue now passes, results match the spmatrix path bit-for-bit (up to sign), SpectralClustering is fixed too, and the full test_spectral_embedding.py / test_spectral.py / test_sparse.py suites pass.

Note: the issue speculated this pattern (sparray + accept_large_sparse=False) might affect other estimators (kmeans, svm, coordinate descent, SGD). I checked — those all wrap Cython/C code (libsvm, liblinear, sklearn's own _k_means_lloyd) that genuinely requires 32-bit index buffers, so their restriction is legitimate and out of scope here. Nothing left uncommitted has been staged/committed — let me know if you want it committed or turned into a PR.

</details>

pull_requests.title: MNT Fix _weighted_percentile with nans and average=True
pull_requests.body:
Found that while reviewing https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32761.

_weighted_percentile ignores NaNs by setting their weight to zero on a sorted copy of the weights. In the average=True case, the original sample_weight is used so the weight of a nan is not zero.

Since the sorted nans are always last, only percentile_rank=100 would generate a nan in the output. Hence the extended parametrization of the existing test (it fails on main). 

I don't think it needs a changelog entry because this combination can't be reached from the public API today.

pull_requests.title: feat(inspection): add Accumulated Local Effects (ALE) and AccumulatedLocalEffectsDisplay
pull_requests.body:
### Summary of Changes

Fixes #30223

This PR implements **Accumulated Local Effects (ALE)** for continuous features in `sklearn.inspection`, providing a local-difference alternative to Partial Dependence Plots (PDP) that eliminates extrapolation distortion under correlated features.

### Motivation & Background
As discussed and approved in #30223:
Partial Dependence evaluates marginal expectations $\mathbb{E}_{X_c}[f(x_s, X_c)]$, which forces models to evaluate unrealistic or impossible feature combinations when predictors are strongly correlated.

ALE (Apley & Zhu, 2020) resolves this by:
1. Partitioning continuous feature values into $K$ quantile-based intervals $[z_{k-1}, z_k]$.
2. Evaluating local prediction differences $\Delta f_k(x) = f(z_k, x_{i,c}) - f(z_{k-1}, x_{i,c})$ for samples $x_{i,s}$ actually falling inside each interval.
3. Accumulating local differences across intervals.
4. Mean-centering the accumulated effect so $\mathbb{E}_{X}[\hat{f}_{ALE}(X_s)] = 0$.

### What this PR adds:
1. **Core Engine**: `accumulated_local_effects(estimator, X, features, *, ...)` in `sklearn/inspection/_accumulated_local_effects.py` returning a `Bunch` (`ale`, `values`, `grid_values`, `feature_names`).
2. **Visualization**: `AccumulatedLocalEffectsDisplay` in `sklearn/inspection/_plot/accumulated_local_effects.py` with `.plot()` and `.from_estimator()` adhering to scikit-learn display standards.
3. **Exports**: Exported in `sklearn/inspection/__init__.py`.
4. **Unit Tests**:
   - `test_accumulated_local_effects.py`: Verifies analytical coefficient recovery on 95% correlated linear models, binary & multiclass classification, multi-target regression, sample weights, pandas DataFrame inputs, and input validation.
   - `test_plot_accumulated_local_effects.py`: Verifies `from_estimator`, multi-axis subplots, custom axes, and multiclass target selection.

Signed-off-by: Shikhar Kesharwani <ayushgu02@gmail.com>

pull_requests.title: Bump min deps for 1.10
pull_requests.body:
scikit-learn 1.10 being aimed for early November (RC), I find unlikely that we'll release a 1.9.2 in between (unless 1.9.1 is broken). 

So it's a legit time to bump the min dependencies. A hidden motivation is that bumping scipy min version will allow some nice improvement to speed-up the min doc build (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34939).

I used the following command to bump the dependencies:
``python maint_tools/bump-dependencies-versions.py 2026-11-01``

I chose different versions than what the script would set for scipy and pandas:
- scipy: 1.12.0 -> 1.11.4

pull_requests.title: Feature/fast tree partial dependence plots
pull_requests.body:
This is a draft PR that relates to the issue #28771 .
The partial_dependence function has two methods: "brute" that uses brute force to compute the values exactly and "recursion" that estimate these values using the tree structure. 
The issue discuss the differences in the values returned by the "recursion" and "brute" methods. In fact, a recent paper I published: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14578, shows that the "recursion" method uses same cooperative game as Path Dependent SHAP while the values returned by the "brute" method are defined over the same game as Interventional SHAP. 

This PR introduce the new "tree_accurate" method.
The method does the best of both worlds - it produce the same values as the "brute" while using the tree structure to speed up the computation. The approach is often faster than "brute". Unfortunately is slower than the "recursion" method as it considers the provided data and not just the tree structure.

## The algorithm
Let f1 denote the feature whose partial dependence values we want to compute.

We start with a preprocessing traversal of the tree. This pass considers the background data X and have O(|X| * depth) complexity. (In the extreme case where all nodes split on f1, the complexity is O(|X| * K) where K is the number of nodes in the tree).
For each leaf, we count how many rows from X reach it. For inner nodes that split on f1 the row traverses both right and left. For inner nodes that split on another feature the row traverses right/left according to its split result.

Then we use this count to compute the partial dependence values. This pass consider the grid values and have O(|grid| * K) complexity.
For each grid value we traverse the tree, going both right and left on splits that does not use f1 and right/left according to its split result for splits that use f1. Each reached leaf contributes to the value: leaf_weight * count[leaf]/|X|

The algorithm is implemented in the compute_partial_dependence_tree_accurate function in _tree.pyx

## Benchmarking
For benchmarking, I used the California housing dataset. I split it 80/20 with random_state=0, the trainset have 16512 rows and 8 features. I trained RandomForestRegressor models with 100 trees and depths 8/16/32 on this trainset and compute the partial dependence values of MedInc (the dominant feature) using difference grid resolutions and the entire trainset as reference data.

`tree_accurate` and `recursion` are timed best-of-3 after a warmup. `brute` is measured twice — **sequential** (`n_jobs=1`,
which is the scikit-learn default, since `RandomForestRegressor` ships with
`n_jobs=None` and `_partition_estimators` resolves that to 1) and **parallel**
(`n_jobs=-1`, spreading the 100 trees across cores). 

I run it on my laptop: AMD Ryzen 7 5700U (8 physical / 16 logical cores, 1.8 GHz base), 37.8 GB RAM. Python 3.12.7, NumPy 2.4.4, SciPy 1.17.1, joblib 1.5.3, scikit-learn 1.10.dev0

### Timings (ms)

| depth | grid | tree_accurate | recursion | brute seq | brute par | brute seq / tree_accurate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 5 | 430.5 | 3.1 | 315.6 | 276.2 | 0.7x |
| 8 | 20 | 431.9 | 2.7 | 1258.7 | 1126.7 | 2.9x |
| 8 | 100 | 431.9 | 4.0 | 6510.3 | 5515.8 | 15.1x |
| 16 | 5 | 1736.1 | 14.3 | 602.5 | 279.7 | 0.3x |
| 16 | 20 | 1746.5 | 27.7 | 2512.5 | 1118.4 | 1.4x |
| 16 | 100 | 1765.4 | 63.3 | 12418.4 | 5664.8 | 7.0x |
| 32 | 5 | 2324.0 | 24.6 | 700.2 | 281.6 | 0.3x |
| 32 | 20 | 2300.6 | 55.6 | 2905.0 | 1097.6 | 1.3x |
| 32 | 100 | 2361.9 | 133.6 | 15785.6 | 5704.3 | 6.7x |

### Accuracy vs `brute` (max absolute difference over the grid)

| depth | grid | tree_accurate | recursion | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 5 | 1.15e-14 | 7.98e-02 | 
| 8 | 20 | 1.42e-14 | 8.66e-02 | 
| 8 | 100 | 1.24e-14 | 8.39e-02 | 
| 16 | 5 | 3.06e-14 | 2.77e-01 | 
| 16 | 20 | 3.82e-14 | 2.77e-01 | 
| 16 | 100 | 5.33e-14 | 2.77e-01 | 
| 32 | 5 | 3.62e-14 | 2.82e-01 | 
| 32 | 20 | 5.68e-14 | 2.82e-01 | 
| 32 | 100 | 6.11e-14 | 2.82e-01 | 

**Notes**:
1. The method supports DecisionTree (Regressor and Classifier),  ExtraTree (Regressor and Classifier), RandomForest (Regressor and Classifier). I can add GradientBoosting and HistGradientBoosting easily if needed.
2. The approach works with multi-output regression and multi-class classification.
3. response_method='decision_function' (or 'auto' when it directs to 'decision_function'). The approach does not support response_method='predict_proba'. I have an idea for supporting predict_proba, but it would require a completely different algorithm.
4. I can easily support sample_weights.
5. The approach currently compute only PDP of a single feature. Joint PDP (tuples of 2 features in the 'features' input) are not supported. I believe the approach can easily be generalized to support them.
6. I did not touched the method="auto" routing yet. We can have it direct to "tree_accurate" instead of "recursion" when possible.

**About myself**: I'm a PhD student researching decision trees explainability. In my PhD I develop faster algorithms for computing explainability methods such as Shapley values, Banzhaf values and partial dependence plots on decision trees. 
I recently worked on the Woodelf algorithm (see https://github.com/ron-wettenstein/woodelf) that computes interventional Shapley/Banzhaf values and Shapley/Banzhaf interaction values, improving the state-of-the-art complexity. Woodelf can also compute partial dependence plots, as discussed in the paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14578, but I think the approach is not a good fit to scikit-learn, as scikit-learn's partial_dependence function accept one feature at a time and Woodelf prefer computing the partial dependence values of all features in one go.

I used claude code (Opus and Fable) for implementation and testing. I read, understood and improved all the code in this PR.

I will be happy to hear your thoughts on this!

pull_requests.title: FIX: Handle single class edge case in balanced_accuracy_score(adjusted=True)
pull_requests.body:
## Issue
Fixes #34889 - `balanced_accuracy_score(adjusted=True)` returns `-inf` when only one class survives NaN filtering.

## Root Cause
The adjustment formula: `score = (score - chance) / (1 - chance)`
When only 1 class survives: 
- `chance = 1/1 = 1.0`
- `denominator = 1 - 1.0 = 0` → division by zero → `-inf`

## Solution
Added validation check to raise informative `ValueError` when only one class is present with `adjusted=True`.

Closes #34889

pull_requests.title: PRF Mitigation heuristics for HGB scalability
pull_requests.body:
Finally, I have something that has a uniformly positive impact on the 8 scenarios I'm testing:
- Big machine with default OMP settings
- Big machine with `OMP_PROC_BIND=close` (avoids penalizing runs that use fewer threads than what's available on the machine)
- Laptop with active wait disabled (the default behavior of conda-forge packages)
- Laptop with active wait enabled

(× libgomp & libomp for each of those)

And it can be very/hugely beneficial in some scenarios (2-10x speed-ups):
- small to medium datasets on a big machine
- small to medium-big datasets on laptops with active wait disabled

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Implements item 4 (partially), item 5 and item 6 of https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34764#issuecomment-5343004000

I'd also say it closes #14306, though that issue does have some ideas that aren't implemented here, in particular parallelizing over blocks of samples × features when building histograms. Benchmarks show HGB does keep scaling up to 16-32 threads for many medium/big datasets, as long as active wait is enabled, which I'd personally consider good enough for now.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

- Detect whether the OpenMP runtime uses active wait, i.e. whether idle threads spin instead of sleeping while waiting for work (`_openmp_uses_active_wait` in `sklearn/utils/_openmp_helpers.pyx`). This is done by parsing the environment dump the runtime prints under `OMP_DISPLAY_ENV=VERBOSE`, in a short-lived subprocess. Active wait makes rejoining a parallel region much cheaper, so all the heuristics below branch on it.
- Cap the number of threads used to grow each tree, based on the number of features and samples (`BaseHistGradientBoosting._get_heurirstic_optimal_n_threads`), instead of always using every available thread.
- Same idea for binning: `_BinMapper`'s `n_threads` parameter is renamed to `max_n_threads` since it's now only an upper bound, the actual thread count used being derived from the amount of data to bin.
- In `Splitter.split_indices`, fall back to a single-threaded partitioning pass when there isn't enough work per thread to justify the chunking/offset bookkeeping of the multi-threaded version.
- In `Splitter.find_node_split`, when active wait is disabled, skip parallelizing over features when there are too few of them relative to `n_threads`.

#### AI usage disclosure

Mostly not, except for the active wait detection: Claude helped find a way to make the subprocess-based `_openmp_uses_active_wait` fast enough not to matter (result cached after the first call, subprocess kept minimal to avoid a full `import sklearn`).

#### Benchmarks

https://pr-81.sklbench-dashboard-preview.pages.dev/

I still have to run some tests on windows.

Current state sphinx warning are turned into errors in PRs and only for files that PRs touch.

The issue is that, in a given PR, some changes to the doc may break references, or similar, in other parts of the doc that are not touched by the PR and so go unnoticed into main.

We recently had 2 examples during the release of 1.9.1 because the CI failed there (it's more likely to fail because the release PR contains many modified files from all the picked commits). see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34915 and https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34916. It's annoying to have to deal with that during the release, but more importantly it's bad that we don't detect it earlier.

This PR proposes to turn all sphinx warnings into errors when we run a full doc build on pushes to main and maintenance branches. Even if we merge a PR that breaks the doc build on main, it won't fire in all PRs because they still only check warnings in the files they modify.

pull_requests.title: MNT Replace deprecated scipy.stats.mstats.mquantiles with np.quantile
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #34926

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`scipy.stats.mstats.mquantiles` is deprecated as of SciPy 2.0.0 and will be removed in SciPy 2.4.0, which is causing `scipy-dev` CI failures (see linked issue for the build log).

The three usages were all in `sklearn/inspection` (grid construction for `partial_dependence`, and decile computation for `PartialDependenceDisplay`). None of them actually needed the masked-array functionality: `X` is always a dense, validated array by the time it reaches these call sites. So I just replaced it with `np.quantile`, using its plain default (linear interpolation).

I checked whether `mquantiles`' default interpolation (Cunnane, `alphap=betap=0.4`, different from `np.quantile`'s `linear`) was a deliberate choice worth preserving. Tracing it back to the original commit that introduced this code in 2012 ([`7f203451a1`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commit/7f203451a1578f811fb88260f4d2c60fabfe6be4), before `_grid_from_X` was even a separate function), `mquantiles` was seemingly picked only because it supported an `axis` argument — `np.percentile` didn't gain one until NumPy 1.9 (2014). There's no discussion anywhere of the interpolation scheme itself. So this looks like an incidental implementation detail rather than a deliberate statistical choice, and I went with `np.quantile`'s current plain default rather than trying to match the old behavior more closely.

No public behavior change: this is an internal implementation swap. Grid/decile values may shift by small floating-point amounts due to the different (but standard) interpolation scheme.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation
- Test/benchmark generation
- Research and understanding

pull_requests.title: PERF Vectorize sparse path of PolynomialCountSketch.transform
pull_requests.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
See #34920 (not using a closing keyword since the issue is still pending
triage).

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
`PolynomialCountSketch.transform`'s sparse branch loops over every feature
and every degree, slicing one sparse column at a time and calling
`.toarray()` on it:

```python
for j in range(X_gamma.shape[1]):
    for d in range(self.degree):
        iHashIndex = self.indexHash_[d, j]
        iHashBit = self.bitHash_[d, j]
        count_sketches[:, d, iHashIndex] += (
            (iHashBit * X_gamma[:, [j]]).toarray().ravel()
        )
```

This densifies a full `(n_samples,)` array on every iteration regardless of
column sparsity, so cost scales with `n_features * degree` instead of the
number of nonzeros. On a 1%-density matrix with a few thousand features, the
sparse path ends up an order of magnitude slower than just densifying the
whole input and using the dense branch.

This PR replaces the double loop with one sparse matrix multiplication per
degree: scale columns by `bitHash_[d, :]` via `.multiply(...)`, then
scatter-sum into buckets with a sparse 0/1 projection matrix built from
`indexHash_[d, :]`. Output is unchanged.

Local benchmark (2000 samples, 300 components, degree=2, 1% density):

| n_features | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1000 | 0.097s | 0.002s |
| 4000 | 0.323s | 0.005s |
| 8000 | 0.631s | 0.009s |

**Important: this PR always improves on the code it replaces.** The table
below (1000 samples, 200 components, degree=2, 2000 features, varying
density) makes both comparisons explicit — old-vs-new (the one that matters
for approval) and new-vs-dense (context on the sparse/dense crossover):

| density | old sparse | new sparse | old vs new | new vs dense |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.1% | 0.151s | 0.002s | **75x faster** | 0.15x (beats dense) |
| 1% | 0.155s | 0.002s | **78x faster** | 0.18x (beats dense) |
| 10% | 0.151s | 0.008s | **19x faster** | 0.69x (beats dense) |
| 30% | 0.156s | 0.017s | **9x faster** | 1.45x (slower than dense) |
| 50% | 0.161s | 0.022s | **7x faster** | 1.98x (slower than dense) |
| 80% | 0.162s | 0.030s | **5x faster** | 2.70x (slower than dense) |

The old sparse path was uniformly ~0.15-0.16s *regardless of density*,
because its cost was driven by loop count (`n_features * degree`) rather
than the data itself. The new path's cost scales with the number of
nonzeros, so it is dramatically faster than the old path at every density
tested — 5x to 78x depending on density — even though at high density (>~20%)
it is still somewhat slower than simply densifying the input and using the
unrelated dense branch, which is expected of any sparse algorithm and not a
regression: a 50-80%-dense matrix stored as a sparse type is already an
unusual choice on the caller's part, and the fix never makes that case worse
than main, only better.

Note on dense input: the `else` branch handling dense arrays is untouched by
this PR (byte-for-byte identical diff), and measured dense `transform` timing
is unchanged before/after within run-to-run noise.

Since this is a performance fix rather than a correctness bug, the existing
`test_polynomial_count_sketch_dense_sparse` test passes on both the old and
new implementation (both are correct, just different speeds), so it alone
doesn't prove the new code is right. I added
`test_polynomial_count_sketch_sparse_edge_cases`, covering all-zero sparse
columns and a single-feature/single-sample input, shapes not exercised by the
existing random test data. I confirmed this new test is not vacuous: I
temporarily broke the new vectorized code (dropped the sign-hash multiply)
and the new test failed with a clear mismatch, then restored the fix.

Verification:
- `pytest sklearn/tests/test_kernel_approximation.py` -> 80 passed
- `check_estimator(PolynomialCountSketch())` passes
- `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` clean

#### Introduce yourself
I use scikit-learn for general ML work. While checking the open-issue
backlog for something to contribute, I found it heavily claimed (most open
`Bug`/`Documentation`/`good first issue`/`help wanted` issues already had a
competing PR or an active claim comment), so I looked for an improvement by
reading source directly instead, and found this inefficiency in
`kernel_approximation.py`.

#### AI usage disclosure
I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (e.g., when writing an implementation or fixing a bug)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Research and understanding

#### Any other comments?
Already added the `efficiency` changelog entry under
`doc/whats_new/upcoming_changes/sklearn.kernel_approximation/34919.efficiency.rst`.

Opened #34920 to report the bug ahead of this PR per the contributing
guidelines. It's pending triage, so this PR references it without a closing
keyword for now and I'll switch to `Fixes #34920` once the label is cleared.

pull_requests.title: PERF New parallelism API with lower overhead
pull_requests.body: `joblib.Parallel` has significant performance overhead. `sklearn.utils.parallel.Parallel` has even more. That means parallelism becomes pointless in some cases, because the overhead of using these APIs drowns out the benefits of parallelism. This PR introduces a new parallelism API with lower overhead, and switches the IsolationForest prediction algorithm to use it instead of `Parallel()` as a demonstration of the benefits. ### Background https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/28622 introduced parallelism for IsolationForest prediction. However, it did _not_ enable parallelism by default, because for smaller samples the overhead made the parallel version slower. ### Speed-up of `IsolationForest` enabled by this PR With this PR, the speed of predicting large number of samples is essentially the same (so I omitted this from the plots below because it obscures the improvements on small numbers of samples). However, because of lower overhead: * Parallelism is now almost always faster than parallelism. Even in the worst case, previously it was much faster in the 100 samples case, now it's only slightly worse given how much faster all of this is for 100 samples. * For smaller number of samples, the lower overhead speeds up results. Here's a plot of before and after using this API, generated with `bench_plot_isolation_forest_predict.py` (with the 50,000 sample case disabled; for that value there's no benefit in the new API): ### Question for reviewers Since parallelism is now useful in almost all cases, and less harmful when it's not, it is worth turning it on by default? ### AI: None ### Future work * New APIs can now be parallelized, e.g. on free-threading; see #34747 which I will update and resubmit if/when this PR gets merged. * Swapping out `ThreadPoolExecutor` for a faster thread pool (e.g. https://github.com/Quansight/spinningjenny/) can reduce parallelism overhead even more. See numbers in #34747 for an example.

pull_requests.body:
# WIP: still cleaning the diff, fixing tests, ...

Finally, I have something that has a uniformly positive impact on the 8 scenarios I'm testing:
- Big machine with default OMP settings
- Big machine with default OMP_PROC_BIND=close => this setting is somewhat representative of [TODO]
- Laptop with no active wait enabled (behavior of conda-forge packages)
- Laptop with active wait

(x Libgomp & libomp for each of those cases)

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Implements item 4 partially, and item 5 of https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34764#issuecomment-5343004000

And I'd say it also closes https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/14306. Though this issues does have some interesting idea that are not implemented here, especially parallelism over block of samples x features for the histogram building. Still, benchmarks show HGB does continue to scale until 16-32 threads for many medium/big datasets (as long as active wait is enabled). I personally would consider that good enough ^^

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

- Limit number of threads for tree-growth based on number of features and some heuristics
- Use a serialized implementation of apply split when the number of samples is small compared to the number of threads => this makes apply split scales as well as it can (scale when possible, do not regress otherwise)
- Some limitations on the number of threads for the binning

#### AI usage disclosure: mostly not

#### Benchmarks

https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks/pull/74

Except one case regressing on the GNR that is probably due to numa placement (see https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks/issues/80), no regression further than ~5% and some very neat improvements (especially on the GNR).

You'll see the no-active-wait set-ups still scale very counter-productively in many cases, I plan to try tackling that in a follow-up PR. Current plan:
- detect active wait, either by reading some logs (a bit slow), or by probing.
- maybe? for libomp, use `set_kmp_block_time` to actually enable active wait (maybe dangerous if inside outer parallelism) 
- then adapt heuristics and/or warn users about what they should do (maybe link to documentation?)

For the scalability on machines like the GNR, it's still not perfect but I don't think it's worth improving more than that.
